items.title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
items.summary: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
items.content:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.

Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.

However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.

On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.

But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.

The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.

Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.

The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.

In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.

In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.

The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.

A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.

US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".

However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.

Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.

"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.

"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."

Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.

"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.

"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.

"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck

As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.

And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.

Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.

Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.

"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

items.title: A Potenza "chiude" il ponte Musmeci, gioiello del '900
items.summary: Degrado impone lo stop alle auto. Una gara europea per salvarlo
items.content: Una rete arancione da cantiere a sbarrare l'acceso segna una svolta dolorosa per la mobilità e la storia di Potenza. A seguito delle segnalazioni dei Vigili del Fuoco per il distacco e la caduta di calcinacci dalle strutture del viadotto, il Comune ha disposto la chiusura immediata al transito veicolare del Ponte Musmeci. L'infrastruttura, snodo strategico di accesso al capoluogo lucano, chiude temporaneamente sotto il peso del tempo e dell'usura, riaprendo le polemiche sullo stato di conservazione, a lungo ignorato, di una grande opera dell'uomo. Perché quel viadotto non è solo un tratto di strada concepito per scavalcare la linea ferroviaria e il Parco del fiume Basento, ma è un capolavoro mondiale dell'ingegneria del Novecento, prima opera d'arte infrastrutturale in Italia riconosciuta il 2 dicembre 2003 come "Monumento di interesse culturale" e sottoposto a vincolo ministeriale. Progettato nel 1967 e completato nel 1975 dal geniale ingegnere Sergio Musmeci, il ponte ha una forma assolutamente caratteristica: priva dei tradizionali piloni, la struttura portante consiste in una membrana continua di cemento armato, fatta di dossi e avvallamenti, sulla quale è adagiato il piano stradale. La chiusura forzata del ponte mette a nudo un paradosso: da un lato un'icona dell'ingegneristica moderna, dall'altro lato l'incuria protratta nel tempo, che oggi impone urgenti e costosi interventi di restauro e consolidamento statico di un'opera simbolo del genio umano. Una gara d'appalto europea è già in corso: l'intervento, che dovrà essere affidato a un'impresa con altissime competenze tecniche, è sostenuto da un finanziamento della Regione Basilicata pari a 11 milioni di euro, destinati a coprire anche le spese di progettazione avanzata, l'implementazione tecnologica e i costi accessori. Ma l'orizzonte temporale per il completamento delle opere non è vicino, stimato intorno al 2030. Mentre si spera che le verifiche tecniche già in corso consentano una riapertura almeno parziale del viadotto, inevitabilmente Potenza da subito deve fare i conti con una riorganizzazione significativa della viabilità in entrata e in uscita dalla città.

items.title: Copernicus: 'Il mese di ottobre è stato il più caldo mai registrato'
items.summary: Il 2026 sforerà il limite di riscaldamento di 1,5°C dell'Accordo di Parigi
items.content:
L'ottobre del 2026 è stato, a livello globale, l'ottobre più caldo mai registrato , con una temperatura media di 1,75 gradi centigradi superiore al livello preindustriale (1850-1900). Lo rende noto il servizio meteo della Ue, Copernicus. E' stato il terzo mese consecutivo a superare la soglia di 1,5 gradi. E' praticamente certo che la temperatura media globale del 2026 supererà di oltre 1,5 gradi il livello preindustriale, sforando il limite più ambizioso posto dall'Accordo di Parigi sul clima. Con un intervallo previsto compreso tra 1,56 gradi e 1,61, il 2026 diventerebbe il secondo anno solare, dopo il 2024, a superare la soglia di 1,5 gradi.

Secondo Copernicus, è molto probabile che il 2026 diventi il secondo anno più caldo mai registrato, con una probabilità di circa l'80%, mentre esiste una possibilità del 20% che eguagli o superi il 2024, attualmente l'anno più caldo mai registrato. Si prevede inoltre che la temperatura globale media del quadriennio 2023-2026 supererà di oltre 1,5°C i livelli preindustriali. A ottobre, la temperatura della superficie del mare si è mantenuta su livelli eccezionalmente elevati. Al di fuori delle regioni polari, la temperatura media della superficie marina ha raggiunto i 20,95°C, il valore più alto mai registrato per il mese di ottobre , superando il precedente record stabilito nell'ottobre 2023. Nel Pacifico tropicale, dove le condizioni legate a El Niño hanno continuato a intensificarsi, l'anomalia mensile della temperatura superficiale del mare nella regione Niño 3.4 ha toccato un massimo storico di 3,21°C, superando i picchi osservati durante i precedenti episodi di El Niño di forte intensità.

Nel frattempo, l'Europa ha vissuto il suo secondo ottobre più caldo mai registrato. A differenza di quanto accaduto a settembre e durante gran parte dell'estate , le temperature hanno fatto registrare gli scostamenti più significativi rispetto alla media nell'Europa orientale e in Scandinavia, mentre in gran parte dell'Europa occidentale e centrale le anomalie termiche positive sono risultate più contenute. In gran parte dell'Europa centrale e orientale hanno persistito portate fluviali eccezionalmente basse, che hanno interessato il Reno, il Danubio e la Vistola. In alcune zone dell'Europa occidentale, invece, la portata dei fiumi ha registrato una ripresa, grazie a un'attenuazione delle condizioni di siccità nel mese di ottobre rispetto a settembre . Forti precipitazioni e inondazioni hanno colpito diversi Paesi, tra cui il Regno Unito, l'Irlanda, la Spagna, la Grecia e la Turchia.

items.title: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.planned-obsolescence.org/p/ai-is-dramatically-accelerating-ai Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50397994 Points: 206 # Comments: 157
items.content:
This post discusses a public METR report on AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic. I did not work on this project or see the unredacted report. 1 All opinions are my own and do not represent METR or the report authors. Thanks to Ryan Greenblatt for discussion, feedback, and help with modeling, and Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, and Hjalmar Wjik for comments.

Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026) , say this threshold will be met when:

They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D. 2

This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs. 3

For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed. 4

Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative."

While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted.

This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack . Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team ) have projected.

Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that.

Researchers work on improving algorithms and architectures; Anthropic has sometimes referred to these innovations as “compute multipliers.” 5 Overall AI capabilities (“effective compute”) is the product of compute multipliers and training compute. Because the compute multipliers are only one input into capabilities, this means that if AI capabilities are advancing twice as fast overall because of software progress, the rate of growth in compute multipliers would need to be more than twice as fast: perhaps ~2.5-3x faster based on reasonable assumptions. 6 Since there’s uncertainty about the size of speedup and how much of it comes from AI, I’ll go with ~2-3x.

Similarly, researcher labor is only one input to discovering these compute multipliers: they need to test their ideas, which requires compute for experiments. If we assume a very simple Cobb-Douglas model where experiment compute and labor are similarly important, that means the uplift to labor roughly needs to be the square of the acceleration in compute multipliers. 7 This would imply that we would need a (~2-3x)^2 = ~4-9x speed up in labor to make overall AI capabilities go twice as fast. 8

However, once capabilities start speeding up significantly, this also means that low-hanging fruit is plucked at a correspondingly faster rate. Each new compute multiplier takes more and more work to discover and implement (i.e., “ideas are getting harder to find”). Before there was much acceleration from AI, labor roughly grew at some roughly fixed exponential rate from hiring more humans. Combined with growth in compute, this compensated for diminishing returns enough to maintain the baseline rate of capabilities progress. But to maintain a new faster rate of capabilities progress without scaling compute faster, we would need a new faster rate of growth in overall labor.

Since the human labor force is stuck growing at more or less the old rate, the uplift from AI would need to get larger and larger over time just to sustain capabilities progress at its new rate. That means the uplift today, after several months of accelerated progress from AI, 9 needs to be even higher than ~4-9x, the estimate for what it would take to double progress at the start: maybe the necessary labor uplift is ~10x . This is very uncertain, and substantially more or less is plausible. But it lines up surprisingly well with informal self-reports from Anthropic staff, who say they are now getting a ~12x uplift from the use of internal models.

When you’re picturing a 10x uplift, you should not be imagining that every researcher is now a team of ten researchers — as anyone who has ever done anything knows, a team of ten does not get ten times as much valuable work done per hour as one person. Instead, it’s as if every researcher at Anthropic is in a time warp bubble where they experience ten days for every day that passes in the outside world . As if AI lets them think, read, speak, type, and do everything else ten times faster. 10 Anthropic probably wouldn’t have been able to speed up its research this much by hiring any number of people. 11

A reasonable default expectation is that as AI capabilities continue to improve, AI researchers will be sped up more and more from automation: if today it takes them a month to get as much work done as they used to in a year, soon it will take a week, and then perhaps a day. If this increasing labor uplift is strong enough to overcome diminishing returns, then in the absence of other bottlenecks it would translate into even larger speed ups in the rate of AI progress: progress will start going 4x faster, and then 8x, and then 16x, and so on.

The report authors were very uncertain about this question, and say that their picture changed several times with new information. But ultimately, they did not find evidence of bottlenecks or steep diminishing returns that would get in the way of compounding acceleration. 12 They also report seeing some (confusing) redacted evidence indicating that acceleration could already be above 2x and increasing over time.

If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year. It seems that around a year’s worth of AI progress got us from modest acceleration to the point where AIs now make AI progress roughly twice as fast. If acceleration from AI is smoothly increasing, then at this new rate, we should expect that we will double the rate of progress again within six months. At that point, it would take three months to double it again, then six weeks. 13

In theory, these doubling times would add up to infinite capabilities within one year. In reality, at some point we would reach the effective ceiling on software efficiency . But I expect these limits to be very far from where we are now.

If we go through this feedback loop, I expect that the AI systems that come out the other side will be able to very quickly develop novel weapons and very easily overpower human civilization in a conflict. If these systems were seriously misaligned, I think they would likely disempower humanity , and this could lead to human extinction.

The “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” is such an important and extreme milestone because it is a strong concrete indicator of extreme capabilities in the very near term. Indeed, in an earlier version of Anthropic’s RSP (May 2025) , the highest named risk threshold for AI research automation (AI R&D-5) corresponded to a somewhat weaker milestone. 14 According to the old RSP, Anthropic would be required to have, at a minimum, security good enough to “protect against model-weight theft by state-level adversaries” 15 by the time it reached AI R&D-5.

I agree that very strong security, both for model weights and algorithmic secrets themselves, is a minimum prerequisite for undergoing an intelligence explosion next year without running very large risks of killing billions of people. The AI industry is nowhere near this bar: both OpenAI and Anthropic recently had major security breaches by amateur groups. Beyond strong model weight security, I also think we would need robust logging and monitoring with universal coverage, reliable measurements of monitorability , effective countermeasures against monitor collusion , principled alignment training techniques with very convincing model organisms or interpretability to understand how well they’re working, governance infrastructure for pacing progress if we notice these alignment and control interventions start to break down…and many other measures if we’re going to approach an intelligence explosion in anything like a responsible way.

items.title: Google has acquired Crusoe's data center site in southeast Wyoming
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/newsroom/crusoe-wyoming-data-center-campus-update Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50397711 Points: 41 # Comments: 7
items.content:
Google has acquired Crusoe’s data center site in southeast Wyoming, completing Crusoe’s pre-development work on site selection, governmental approvals, and a hybrid power strategy developed with Tallgrass Energy.

DENVER — November 6, 2026 — Crusoe, the AI factory company, today announced its site in southeast Wyoming has been acquired by Google. The transaction marks the completion of Crusoe's engagement in pre-development work on the Wyoming project – which included data center site selection, governmental approvals, and power strategy.

"Crusoe’s pre-construction efforts – origination, entitlement, and de-risking – have set up the Wyoming project for construction and eventual operation,” said Chase Lochmiller, Co-founder and CEO of Crusoe. “Crusoe is in the business of activating gigawatts for intelligence. With more than 6 GW contracted and over 40 GW in our pipeline, we are eager to steward the development and energization of the foundational infrastructure of AI.”

Crusoe and Tallgrass Energy initiated the Wyoming campus through the joint development of power and data center infrastructure. This parallel process required simultaneous coordination across energy systems design, data center engineering, site development, and hyperscaler engagement. The innovative hybrid power strategy developed for the campus exemplifies Crusoe’s integrated approach to digital infrastructure, combining fuel cells, grid power, and natural gas turbines with a long-term roadmap for carbon capture via Tallgrass’s regional CO2 sequestration hub.

Crusoe recently announced it is the developer of Google’s data center campus under construction in Armstrong County outside of Amarillo.

As the AI factory company, Crusoe is on a mission to accelerate the abundance of energy and intelligence. The company provides a reliable, scalable, cost-effective, energy-first solution for AI infrastructure. By harnessing large-scale energy sources, building AI-optimized data centers, and delivering a powerful AI cloud platform, Crusoe empowers its customers and partners to build the future faster. For more information, visit crusoe.ai.

items.title: Midterm: Trump torna all'attacco, 'non mollerò mai'. E nomina Miller capo dello staff
items.summary: Wiles prima testa a cadere. Il tycoon: 'Tonfo Wall Street colpa dei dem, distruggo l'Iran'
items.content:
Donald Trump, incassata in parte la delusione per la sonora sconfitta subita alle midterm, non cede e torna all'attacco, lanciando un chiaro avvertimento: "Non mi arrenderò mai". Malgrado la pesante batosta, il tycoon ritrova energie e spara ad alzo zero contro i democratici, accusandoli del 'giovedì nero' di Wall Street. E, mentre dietro le quinte si tratta, rispolvera le minacce all'Iran: 'O fanno l'accordo o li distruggo'. Intanto, nell'ambito della resa dei conti apertasi alla Casa Bianca e all'interno del partito repubblicano, cade la prima testa: è quella del capo dello staff del presidente Susie Wiles.

Al suo posto Trump ha nominato Steven Miller, suo fedelissimo e architetto delle politiche trumpiane sull'immigrazione, assecondando così le richieste giunte da una parte dei leader del movimento Maga. Il contraccolpo del voto sui mercati finanziari da al tycoon lo spunto per sferrare il primo vero attacco ai democratici dalle elezioni: è colpa loro se Wall Street ha vissuto quella che definisce "una delle giornate peggiori della sua storia".

Perché lo tsunami blu ha mandato in fumo 3.200 miliardi di dollari di capitalizzazione messi insieme "con un impegno enorme", per colpa - accusa - dei propositi dem di regolamentare Big Tech. Il tycoon, poi, rivendica "al 100%" il pieno supporto alla Super Intelligenza, convinto che "sia miope" non dotarsene, a dispetto della chiara bocciatura dei data center emersa dalle urne in tutto il Paese. Sull'Iran, poi, il tycoon appare indeciso, ma torna a usare parole dure: "Vogliamo andare oltre e limitarci a certificare l'accordo, il che significherebbe che una cosa del genere non accadrà mai più...Oppure possiamo distruggere il resto del Paese, ma preferirei non farlo, se possibile. Ma forse sarò costretto, lo saprete presto".

Nel frattempo ha riunito per la prima volta nel dopo midterm i consiglieri per la sicurezza nazionale. Mentre i media americani hanno dato conto del pressing del vicepresidente Jd Vance per una soluzione negoziale con Teheran, il primo punto del suo programma di rifondazione della destra Usa in vista delle presidenziali del 2028. Secondo Axios, il presidente, almeno per ora, valuta tre opzioni: lanciare nuovi attacchi (secondo Fox News il 9 novembre, con la luna nuova), continuare a strangolare economicamente il regime iraniano o raggiungere un accordo che includa significative concessioni a favore di Teheran. Il tutto nel mezzo dell'intensa attività diplomatica, incluse le numerose telefonate tra il ministro degli Esteri iraniano Abbas Araghchi e i mediatori regionali di Qatar, Arabia Saudita, Turchia, Emirati Arabi Uniti, Oman ed Egitto. Poi c'è la resa di conti nel partito. Il tracollo elettorale repubblicano ha aperto la battaglia per le primarie del Grand Old Party con vista sul 2028: Vance è finito sotto accusa per aver attribuito il disastro delle urne alla guerra in Iran, dimenticandosi "dei dazi e del costo della vita" (ha rilevato il Wall Street Journal), e altri esponenti di spicco del partito sembrano voler prendere le distanze dall'amministrazione, definendo le proprie posizioni.

Si è già creato, in altri termini, un ampio margine di manovra per gli aspiranti candidati alla Casa Bianca, tra cui il governatore della Florida Ron DeSantis e il senatore del Texas Ted Cruz, per contrapporsi a Vance. Mentre il segretario di Stato Marco Rubio, a dispetto della smentita sulla sua uscita dall'amministrazione Trump per la corsa del 2028, appare in condizioni leggermente migliori su Vance: ma il peso negativo del voto di martedì potrebbe essere per entrambi un peso insormontabile, dato che le elezioni hanno rappresentato un vero e proprio referendum sul loro operato. Trump intanto, incassando i dati più che positivi sull'occupazione di ottobre, continua a raccogliere fondi per le sue attività politiche con un obiettivo ben preciso: Axios - secondo cui il tycoon continua ad alimentare i suoi Super Pac, come Maga Inc - ha riferito che The Donald punta ad avere la forza per influenzare gli scenari del 2028, mettendo sotto pressione i repubblicani che vorrebbero rompere con lui. Infine, la posizione del capo del Pentagono Pete Hegseth appare sempre più complicata: il deputato repubblicano Thomas Massie, deciso oppositore di Trump, presenterà la prossima settimana, alla ripresa dei lavori del Congresso, la mozione di impeachment contro il segretario alla Difesa. "C'è un solo scenario in cui non la ripresenterò: se Hegseth si dimette", ha scritto Massie in un post su X.

items.title: A Jev that can ask Opus for help gives Opus accuracy at 4x lower cost
items.summary: Article URL: https://hightouch.com/blog/llm-judges-identity-resolution Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50397429 Points: 339 # Comments: 73
items.content:
We wanted to test whether LLMs and decision models, specifically Jev and Luna, could solve a hard problem that we encounter regularly (grading identity resolution results). We found that while both models performed okay out of the box (88.8–97.3% accuracy), implementing a hybrid model that combines Jev + Opus achieves frontier accuracy at > 4x lower costs.

Identity resolution is the process of mapping data to corresponding real people. More precisely, say you have a set of data records D . Determine a set of identities I and mapping m(D)->I such that each record d ∈ D maps to an identity i ∈ I , each i corresponds to exactly one real person in the real world, and no two i correspond to the same person in the real world.

This is foundational for any company wishing to do outreach, personalization, or analytics on customers. You can’t know, for instance, the lifetime value of a customer without being able to map all their purchases to a single identity.

For example, the input data might contain the following records. IDR would ideally create one identity, Alice , and associate all of these records with Alice .

In practice, IDR is very difficult. People share emails, move addresses, etc. There might also be errors in the data. See some examples here:

The most common and problematic issue with IDR is over-merging . This is when an identity i incorrectly corresponds to multiple people in the real world.

On real data, there is no answer key we can consult after we’ve merged records into identities. If there were, then we'd just use that to match data, and we wouldn't need to do IDR. This makes it very difficult to assess the accuracy of any IDR algorithm. In practice, teams will spend months attempting to determine if their IDR is working.

You can use heuristics to look for statistical signs of over-merged profiles (count the number of emails per identity, etc), but ultimately you need to sample output identities and review them by hand to know how well your IDR algorithm is performing.

To do this, we define the records Dᵢ as the set of d such that m(d) -> i for any given i . If the IDR engine is successful, then we should only find evidence of one real person in any given Dᵢ .

Human sampling is slow (~50 identities/hr), and sampling small numbers of identities gives poor estimates of over-merging. Over-merges are rare in a healthy graph, and estimating a rare rate precisely takes more samples than people expect (> 1000 samples to get the error down to under +-1% on over-merging rate)

An LLM should, intuitively, be able to replicate what a human is doing when they inspect an identity. If a model can judge identities at human accuracy, then we could spin up as many LLMs as we want to grade identities in parallel. A sample of 100,000 identities could be evaluated in seconds. This would enable much faster iteration cycles when setting up IDR, and make maintenance much easier.

Of particular interest are Jev and GPT-6 Luna . These are members of a new class of language models that return a 0-1 confidence score that a specific condition is true. They are far faster and cheaper than current frontier models.

We made a benchmark with pseudopeople , a tool from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington. It simulates a fictional US town and generates records of its residents from multiple sources. We also added a bunch of realistic data errors.

From those records, we built 1,000 identities. Half are one person with noisy records, and half are over-merges. Then we spun up some models and measured how they did.

Then we described the kinds of noise in the data, so that a typo would not be mistaken for a new person:

Every model gained the most from the error examples. The data context then added at most a point for the frontier models and wasn't helpful for the decision models. Our guess is that decision models don't really reason, so providing fundamental context doesn't help them. We kept the full prompt for all models to keep things consistent. With the final prompt, the results were:

Initially, we used a 50% confidence threshold, but this was arbitrary. We can adjust it to trade one type of error for another.

The cutoff matters a lot for Jev and very little for Luna. We settled on 60% for Jev and 70% for Luna, which maximize accuracy in each case. Here’s how both models perform with a better-calibrated threshold.

So far Luna looks very good; indeed, it's surprisingly close to the frontier models at a small fraction of their cost. We decided to up the difficulty of our test to see if the frontier models could pull ahead.

We used the same town and the same kinds of noise, but only tricky cases. We tried to trick the model by constructing cases including:

Great, there's a clear gap between the frontier models and Luna now. Interestingly, Luna is also now level with Jev, despite being ahead previously. We started digging into the cases where Luna and Jev got it wrong to see whether we could improve accuracy without paying for a frontier model.

In investigating the cases in which Jev and Luna missed while the larger models got it right, we noticed a very interesting pattern. Let's start with the easier dataset to see it clearly.

Most of Jev's mistakes are closer to 50% confidence, which is what you'd expect out of a well-calibrated model. Luna, on the other hand, seems quite overconfident in the 90–100% bucket despite making far fewer mistakes.

Let's see what happens when we re-run on the trickier cases.

While Jev's confidence incorrectly shifts higher, its calibration remains far better than Luna's. Luna starts to be spectacularly over-confident here that it has identified an over-merge.

All that matters is that we can, on average, cheaply judge whether an identity is over-merged. We don't have to only rely on one model. If the cheap model is well calibrated, we can forward a small portion of our identities to an expensive model for a second opinion.

Given how overconfident Luna is, we can guess that it won't help Luna as much, but Jev should really be able to take advantage of this.

Not only does this approach bring Jev past Luna in accuracy, but it also almost meets the accuracy of Opus alone. Granted, it’s more expensive than hybrid Luna for pretty similar performance.

Now the gap is very clear. Hybrid Jev's better confidence calibration means it elegantly sends more cases to Opus on harder data without any harness or prompting change. We pay more, but it's a system that will automatically scale spend when needed to maintain accuracy, which is what we want. It's also still way cheaper than Opus alone. While Luna appears to do better out of the box, its overconfidence condemns it to mediocre performance in the hybrid model.

Calibration matters! Whereas Luna works better out of the box, its overconfidence prevents success on harder datasets. The hybrid approach is clearly useful, and we suspect it's not just useful in this domain.

Hybrid Jev's ability to handle arbitrary problem difficulty is very valuable. You never know how tricky the identities are going to be in practice, so a system that will dynamically flex to spend more when it needs to is awesome.

If we were more cost-sensitive or knew the cases judged were easier, we might pick hybrid Luna, but we think hybrid Jev's advantages are worth the additional costs. We could adjust our thresholds to send fewer cases for a second opinion to bring down costs at the cost of a bit of accuracy in the hybrid Jev approach.

In future posts we'll discuss how we think about under-merging, and look at how performance degrades if we go to open-weight decision models vs. relying on proprietary APIs.

Test data generated with pseudopeople ; no real people appear in any example. Model costs and latencies are what we observed in our own setup and will vary.

items.title: Neonato abbandonato sotto al crocifisso in una chiesa a Roma
items.summary: Sta bene, era in una busta. Nei video una donna lo lascia e va via
items.content:
Un neonato lasciato all'interno di una busta di plastica della spesa sotto al crocifisso nei pressi dell'altare di una chiesa di Roma. Ad accorgersi che dentro quel sacchetto abbandonato c'era un bambino è stato un parrocchiano che ha dato l'allarme facendo scattare i soccorsi. Sul posto è arrivato il personale dell'Ares 118 e i carabinieri che hanno avviato indagini per risalire a chi ha abbandonato il bimbo.

Intanto la direzione dell'Ares 118 ha voluto rivolgere "il più sincero ringraziamento a tutti i professionisti che, con prontezza, competenza e grande senso di responsabilità, hanno assicurato un intervento tempestivo e un'assistenza attenta al neonato" . "Il loro impegno - ha sottolineato l'Ares - testimonia, ancora una volta, il valore del lavoro quotidiano degli operatori e la loro capacità di rispondere con umanità e professionalità anche alle situazioni più delicate".

items.title: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2
items.summary: Article URL: https://pwn.ai/blog/firecracker-escape Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50397219 Points: 177 # Comments: 77
items.content:
Firecracker is supposed to keep untrusted code inside a microVM. We escaped it and achieved code execution as root on the host.

We found how it saved registers, changed where it would resume, and made it execute a call of our choosing when it returned from KVM. The guest then restored the temporary stack changes. Firecracker kept running, and the VM remained accessible over SSH.

PwnEscape Part 1 introduced the host memory primitive behind this work. Here we follow the next part of the chain: using that access to find Firecracker in memory and take over a live thread from inside the guest. This is a continuation to show CVE-2026-99999 on a Firecracker setup.

A Firecracker microVM has a process on the host that manages it. Each virtual CPU, or vCPU, has a thread in that process. The thread enters KVM to run the guest and returns to Firecracker when an event needs handling in userspace. Firecracker documents this arrangement in its architecture overview .

While the thread is in that system call, the host kernel holds its saved userspace registers in a structure called pt_regs . These registers describe the Firecracker thread: its instruction pointer says where execution should resume, and its stack pointer says which userspace stack it should use.

That made the return from KVM_RUN an attractive target. If we could locate and modify the saved frame, we could choose the code Firecracker executed when the thread returned to userspace. A guest operation that caused such a return would provide the trigger.

We already had access to selected host physical memory through a guest mapping. To use it, we needed to identify the Firecracker process, find code we could call in that process, and locate the register frame belonging to its active vCPU thread. The starting point was a page of memory we controlled inside the guest.

Figure 1. The guest identifies its Firecracker process, finds the saved registers for a vCPU thread, and redirects the thread when it returns from KVM.

The guest and host use different physical address spaces. A page has a guest physical address, or GPA, inside the VM and a host physical address, or HPA, in the machine backing it. On the target, Extended Page Tables (EPT) provide the translation between them.

We placed a recognizable byte pattern, a nonce, in a guest page. The first resolver took that page's known GPA and its contents as inputs. Together, they gave us an address to translate and a way to check whether the translation reached our page.

The resolver searched the host physical ranges covered by the memory primitive for candidate EPT roots. An EPT root is the starting point of the translation tables. For each candidate, the resolver followed the entries selected by the guest address until it reached a physical page, then checked that page for the nonce.

The snippets below are explanatory pseudocode with descriptive helper names. They show the data passed between stages and the checks used to connect them.

The nonce check connected a proposed translation to memory we controlled. The broader search produced two candidates; validation of the nested page tables reduced them to one EPT root. Walking that root gave us the host physical address of our guest page.

We called this result guest_page_hpa and passed it to the next resolver. We now had a recognizable object in host memory. The next task was finding the host process that mapped it.

Firecracker maps memory used by the guest into its own address space. That mapping gave us a way to work backward from the guest page to the process.

Host processes use page tables to translate their virtual addresses into physical memory. The top level is called the page global directory, or PGD. Recovering the appropriate PGD would let us translate addresses inside Firecracker and read its code and stack through the memory primitive.

Our reverse mapper searched the native host page tables for a mapping of guest_page_hpa . A normal page table walk starts with a virtual address and produces a physical address. Here, we looked for a mapping to a physical page we already knew, then recovered the virtual address and page table root associated with it.

This connected the host process's virtual mapping to the physical page found through EPT. The reverse mapper returned one validated address space. We retained its root as host_pgd and used it to inspect the process.

The next resolver looked for the Firecracker executable in those mappings. It identified an ELF image and checked a known byte sequence in Firecracker's write(2) wrapper. That connected the recovered address space to the binary we were targeting.

ASLR changes where an executable is loaded. The difference between an address in the ELF image and its corresponding runtime address is the load bias. Once the mapper had identified the image, it could recover that bias and use it to locate the code required by the exploit:

The mapper returned the load bias as firecracker_base . With that value and host_pgd , we could locate code in the running process, translate its virtual address to host physical memory, and compare the bytes there with the expected binary.

We checked three locations: the write(2) wrapper that would produce our proof, the continuation after the KVM ioctl, and a short xor eax,eax; ret sequence needed to return cleanly. Their purposes become relevant when we construct the return path below.

At this point, the guest could inspect the Firecracker image and its private mappings. We still needed the saved registers of the thread currently running our VM.

Figure 2. The nonce identifies the guest page in host memory. Its mapping leads to a host page table root, which lets the next resolver locate and validate the Firecracker image.

The frame finder took host_pgd and firecracker_base from the preceding stages. It used them to recognize the host thread's saved state.

The most useful clue was the return address. A vCPU thread in KVM_RUN should have a saved instruction pointer at the corresponding ioctl continuation in Firecracker. We could calculate that address from the validated binary and its load bias.

We then searched host memory for a pt_regs frame consistent with that call. An address match alone would also pick up stale stack contents, so the candidate had to satisfy several related checks:

The stack check tied the frame to the same address space we had recovered from the guest page. The instruction and caller addresses tied it to the Firecracker image. The syscall fields tied it to the operation running the vCPU.

The search left one candidate. Its location was stored as frame_hpa , the host physical address of the saved register frame. We passed it, the PGD, and the load bias to the final helper.

Before changing memory, the helper repeated the code signature, frame, and stack checks. This ensured that the active stage used the same process state the resolvers had identified. The subsequent execution and recovery checks would establish that the selected frame was live.

Figure 3. The candidate register frame must agree with the KVM ioctl, the recovered process page tables, and the validated Firecracker code.

We chose a simple payload: make the Firecracker process write a recognizable string to its own stderr. This would give the host runner an observable result from the process we had taken over.

The string was N8V23M2\n , seven characters followed by a newline. It occupies eight bytes and fits in one stack word. The call we wanted Firecracker to execute was:

Here 2 is Firecracker's stderr file descriptor. The buffer pointer must refer to the string in Firecracker's address space, so we stored the string on its private userspace stack.

We saved three stack words before modifying them. One held the string; the other two held the return addresses for the temporary call sequence. We then changed the saved register frame to supply the wrapper address, its arguments, and a stack pointer for that sequence:

Returning from write also needed care. A successful write of eight bytes returns 8 , while a successful KVM_RUN call returns zero . We placed the address of xor eax,eax; ret first in the return sequence. It clears the return value before the second address brings execution back to Firecracker's original ioctl continuation.

With the stack and saved registers prepared, the guest wrote one byte to its serial port. That operation caused the vCPU thread to return from KVM_RUN . The kernel restored the modified registers, and Firecracker entered the write wrapper with our arguments.

The wrapper emitted the marker, the return sequence cleared eax , and the thread rejoined its original execution path. After control returned to the guest, the helper restored all three stack words.

Figure 4. The saved register frame enters the write wrapper. Two return addresses lead through the return-value adjustment and back into the original Firecracker path.

The host runner captured Firecracker's stderr separately from the guest. The complete output was:

The capture contained exactly eight bytes, including the final newline. Firecracker was still running, guest SSH was responsive, and the helper had restored the three temporary stack words.

items.title: GitHub's new Git storage architecture
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/inside-githubs-new-git-storage-architecture/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50397099 Points: 64 # Comments: 9
items.content:
Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we've demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we've been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.

Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.

We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.

The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.

We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:

Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.

We're already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.

We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:

On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally.

In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We'll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it "Rubicon," a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development.

Let's walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new.

Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica's local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.

Spokes routes a repository's traffic to the same virtual replicas when it can, which keeps their caches warm and latency low, but nothing about correctness depends on a request landing on any particular virtual replica. When a virtual replica goes away, the repository's other virtual replicas keep serving, and a replacement fills its cache as traffic arrives.

When a repository gets busy, we add more virtual replicas. Separately, a fleet of compaction nodes works in the background, directly against Blob Storage and Ref-CAS, to merge each repository's packs and remove unreachable objects. That work never runs on a virtual replica, meaning their CPU and memory can be almost entirely dedicated to serving requests.

Let's walk the architecture from the perspective of a write and a read:

There are many distinct approaches we've taken within the new architecture, from the software stack on the virtual replicas to how traffic routing and workload scheduling are tuned for different use cases (e.g., many small repos vs. one large one). Let's dive deep into two components of the architecture and tell their stories centered on the two design principles.

Object storage services like Azure Blob Storage are incredibly good at what they do, and natural fits for many data-heavy applications like source code storage. They are durable and replicated, hold as much as we need them to, have a relatively low cost per byte, and deliver exceptionally high aggregate throughput so long as traffic is spread across many keys. As a result, nearly everything durable in the new Git storage architecture lives in Azure Blob Storage, including:

Most of that data is written once to a distinct key and never changes afterward, which is what makes it highly suitable for Blob Storage.

References are the opposite. A busy repository's references are a relatively small piece of state that many writes race to update at the same time. That access pattern is harder to serve from Blob Storage, and our first prototypes showed us why. Object storage for this kind of workload is an intuitive choice, and one that works well up to a certain level of scale: conditional writes give a compare-and-swap for free, and the data is already durable and replicated. However, we ran into a difficult set of choices, illustrated below by two approaches we tried.

Our first approach was a write-ahead log for all of a repository's references, indexed by a single blob. Every update is a conditional write against that blob. It's correct, and reads are cheap: a virtual replica asks whether the blob has changed, and if it hasn't, it's done. Writes are where it falls short. Only one conditional write to a blob can be in flight at a time, so even when we batch every push that arrives during a write into the next one, the repository's write ceiling is one write per round trip to a single blob. In practice, this netted us write throughput in the mid-hundreds per second.

Our second approach split the references across several segment blobs, with each reference hashing to one of them. Writes to references in different segments no longer wait on each other, which raises the ceiling. But a read now has to check every segment to know whether anything changed, and it's only as fast as the slowest segment. We'd traded write latency for read latency, and reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. We can visualize this by showing multiple writes and a read side by side:

Neither option met every requirement, so we built something else: a replicated log service dedicated to references, or the Ref-CAS service. This is the (small) consensus group we said at the end of the last post was still somewhere in the stack. Here's how it works.

Each reference update in Ref-CAS is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum. A transaction locks only the references it touches, checks that each one still has the value the writer expects, and becomes visible once a majority of the log's replicas have recorded it. Agents mostly push to their own branches, so most updates don't contend, and they replicate in parallel. When two pushes do update the same reference, only one will append to the log.

Each commit to Ref-CAS gets a log sequence number (LSN), and the repository's version is the LSN of its latest commit. Reads start with a version check against that version. A virtual replica sends the version of the reference state it already holds. If that version is still current, the reply carries no references at all, and an unchanged repository costs a single comparison. If the virtual replica is behind, it gets back the current references and version, along with pointers to pack data and anything else that needs to be known, such as when the last garbage collection cycle occurred.

items.title: Restaurant Delivery Payment-Skimming Campaign
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.infohawk.com/news/2026-11-05-scamwich-restaurant-skimming Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50397017 Points: 96 # Comments: 42
items.content:
InfoHawk research has uncovered a network of 820 suspicious restaurant domains impersonating major US chains, including Jersey Mike's, Jimmy John's, Firehouse Subs, Chipotle, and Dave's Hot Chicken. Some are running sophisticated payment-skimming attacks that capture credit card information and ask customers for their bank's SMS verification codes.

When customers order food online, they expect a familiar experience: find their restaurant, choose their meal, and pay. Increasingly, criminals are exploiting that familiarity by creating convincing clones of restaurant ordering websites, right down to the original site's underlying code.

In early November 2026, InfoHawk researchers investigated a collection of suspicious websites that appear to be part of one or more coordinated restaurant impersonation and payment-skimming operations.

Across two research passes, we identified 820 domains impersonating 35 restaurant brands. Of those, 808 use the .delivery top-level domain, and the rest use .com or .shop .

The scale is concerning, but what makes these sites particularly dangerous is how convincing they can be.

The investigation began with a suspicious domain: mlckessejersstey[.]delivery .

The site impersonated Jersey Mike's, the popular sandwich chain, and reproduced its online ordering experience.

Rather than simply displaying a crude imitation of the restaurant's website, the attackers used a more sophisticated approach: reverse-proxying the legitimate site while replacing the checkout payment form with a malicious one.

A reverse proxy can retrieve content from a legitimate website and present it to visitors under a different domain. This allows an attacker-controlled site to display genuine pages and assets while selectively modifying the parts of the experience that matter to the attacker.

In this case, the malicious checkout requested credit card information and also asked customers for the SMS verification code sent by their bank.

This is a particularly dangerous combination. Capturing a credit card number is valuable to criminals; obtaining a one-time verification code could also help them authorize fraudulent transactions, depending on how the victim's bank uses that code.

For consumers, the experience can appear nearly indistinguishable from ordering directly from the restaurant. The site looks familiar, the menu and ordering flow can behave normally, and the fraudulent payment form appears at the moment a customer expects to pay.

Importantly, this does not require the legitimate restaurant's website to have been hacked. The attackers can operate on infrastructure they control while using the authentic restaurant website as the source of the content they display.

Mostly .delivery typosquats, plus a few look-alike .com and .shop names, found across two research passes. "Seen" is the range of registration or scan dates we have for a brand's domains, all in 2026. Open a brand to see its domains.

Each clone is a reverse proxy : a server that sits between the victim and the real restaurant site, fetches every page from the real site as it is requested, edits it on the way through, and passes it on. Menus, prices, store hours, and the cart are live and correct, because they come from the real site. Only the payment step is replaced. Described from mlckessejersstey[.]delivery (Jersey Mike's); we believe the clones of the other brands run the same kit.

A Google Search ad imitates the restaurant's listing and shows a look-alike domain. The domain is behind Cloudflare, so its real server is hidden, and Cloudflare gives it a valid certificate automatically (Google Trust Services here), so the browser shows "Connection is secure".

The proxy replaces the brand's own host names in pages, scripts, and redirects with the fake domain, and maps each backend to a path on it, such as /__bapi__/ or /__payments__/ . Store lookup, menus, login, and cart all work, because those calls go back through the proxy to the real APIs. Even the brand's own bot-detection script still runs, with its endpoints rewritten.

A few paths are answered by the scammer's server instead of the real site: /js/* (the card form and its scripts) and /payment/socket.io . The form looks like part of checkout. On submit it collects every field (card number, expiry, CVV, name, phone) and sends it, with the site name, to the operator over a live socket.io connection.

We believe a person watching a control panel uses the card elsewhere and, when the bank challenges that payment, tells the victim's page what to show next: "card declined, try another", a page asking for the SMS code ( /js/confirmation/ ), an "approve in your bank app" page ( /js/app/ ), or "invalid code, try again". We believe the code the victim types is what lets the operator's charge through 3-D Secure.

Why this design. The clone never goes out of date, the victim builds a real order with a real total before anything looks wrong, and one kit works against any restaurant by changing the target site, the domain, and a few path rules. The scammer's server does very little work, which makes it cheap to move. Some variants skip the payment wording and only pin the frame's address, re-setting it every time the page changes it.

Searching Google's ad archive (Ads Transparency Center) for the domains in our first sweep found at least 47 Google Search text ads between July 7, 2026, and October 20, 2026, run under at least 46 separate advertiser accounts with at least 43 different, unrelated-looking business names (construction firms, a reptile rescue, a watch company). The ads below are a sub-sample: we searched only for the domains in our first sweep, so there are likely more. Each ad imitates a restaurant's search listing and shows a look-alike domain. Most ran for 1–4 days, usually starting days after the domain was registered.

Most of the clones sit behind Cloudflare (AS13335), which hides the real servers: 761 of the 820 domains use Cloudflare nameservers, 11 use other nameservers, and 48 have none. Another cluster of 68 domains is tied to an Amazon Web Services (AWS) server. Some of its sites are served straight from that server, in Frankfurt ( 3.79.192.101 ) through my-ndns.com nameservers, and its pages carry a different injected script ( /static/ -fix.js ). It uses the same cloning technique, but we found nothing that shows the same people run it, so these sites may come from more than one operator using the same kit.

In our first sweep of 255 domains, 251 were registered at Dynadot, spread across 111 Cloudflare nameserver pairs.

These clones don't need to break into a restaurant's systems. They borrow the real site, page by page, and insert the attack only at the moment a customer pays. That makes them hard to spot from the outside, but it also means the brand's own servers see every page the clone serves. Brands and their ordering providers that watch for their site loading under someone else's domain, or for checkout sessions that never reach the real payment provider, are well placed to catch these sites early.

InfoHawk tracks look-alike domains, the ads that send shoppers to them, and the infrastructure behind them. If you want help detecting attacks like this against your brand, or protecting your website from this cloning technique, get in touch.
